It Risks Getting a Tougher Negotiator.   Plus, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang apologizes to employees and family, and Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong gets more prison time on foreign-collusion charges     President Trump campaigned in Mississippi for Republicans ahead of his party’s midterm losses. CHIP SOMODEVILLA/GETTY IMAGES   In November 2014, days after Democrats suffered a bruising midterm defeat, President Obama traveled to Beijing for an annual gathering of Pacific Rim leaders and a state visit. Xi Jinping, sensing his counterpart’s weakened position, subjected Obama to hours of lectures on Chinese history and governance.

   President Trump is heading to Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit next week, following a midterm loss that was more sweeping than Obama’s. Democrats captured both the House and Senate in what amounted to a repudiation of his presidency . Xi will use the opportunity of hosting APEC to show off China’s tech-driven modernity, even as his team and Trump’s wrangle behind the scenes over plans for an unprecedented three-way meeting involving Trump, Xi and Russian leader Vladimir Putin.

   The parallels are tempting, but the dynamics between these two powers are nothing like those of 2014.

   Back then, “Xi felt confident that the United States under Obama’s leadership wasn’t going to confront the People’s Republic of China,” said Matt Turpin, a visiting fellow at the Hoover Institution who served on Trump’s National Security Council during his first term. China’s economy was still expanding at more than 7% at the time while the post-financial-crisis West struggled, and Washington still embraced free trade with China. The Chinese leader was riding high.

   Trump—and China—in 2026 are different. China’s economy is in far worse shape than it was 12 years ago, and Xi faces his own sensitive political year in 2027, when a leadership reshuffle at the 21st Party Congress will demand his full attention. A volatile relationship with Washington would be the last thing he wants.

   Yet the Chinese leader still can’t seem to resist pressing his leverage , with Beijing’s actions suggesting it may already be overplaying its hand. 

   Since a trade agreement struck a year ago in the South Korean city of Busan, Beijing has fallen short of fulfilling its commitments on agricultural purchases and rare earth exports. In addition, China restricted diesel exports just weeks before the midterm elections. Even though Beijing said the move was aimed at ensuring domestic supply, analysts noted it compounded global energy pressures at a vulnerable political moment for Trump.

   Underscoring Washington’s frustration, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said Friday that they had stressed the importance of China honoring its Busan commitments to Xi’s economic point man, Vice Premier He Lifeng.

   The broken promises will likely alter the dynamic heading into Shenzhen. “I suspect Trump feels that Xi intentionally screwed him on the midterms,” Turpin said. If that’s how Trump sees it, he has little motivation to offer Xi concessions, including on Taiwan, where Beijing earlier this year secured a freeze on U.S. arms sales and has been pressing for rhetorical policy shifts that favor its sovereignty claims over the island.

   Trump’s choice of Stephen Miller, a hard-line immigration architect, to replace Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff also suggests he is more inclined to double down than moderate his approach after the defeat.

   No ‘America Doves’   One alarming dynamic in the bilateral relationship is the absence of moderating voices on the Chinese side. There are only “America hawks” in the Chinese system, Turpin noted—“no ‘America doves.’” That’s even more pronounced under Xi’s consolidation of power, where the internal incentive is always to be tougher on the U.S ., never softer.

   That hawkish consensus is paired with a dangerous blind spot. “Chinese Communist Party leaders really don’t understand the relationship between the president and Congress,” Turpin said. “They largely mirror image and assume the U.S. political system works like theirs.” 

   In other words, Beijing may see the midterm results as an opportunity to extract concessions from a weakened Trump. That could prove a serious miscalculation, pushing a president stung by his midterm defeat toward a harder line on China. 

   On the U.S. side, Turpin expects Democratic congressional leadership to focus on investigating the last two years, uncovering corruption, going after the tech industry, and setting the stage for the 2028 presidential election. Unlike the final years of the Biden administration, when a Republican House worked with a Democratic White House to build a bipartisan consensus on China, Turpin said, the foreign policy energy is more likely to flow toward Israel, Iran and Russia.

   But on one front, the new Democratic majority could make things harder for Beijing. 

   China has long sought the elimination of U.S. restrictions on high-tech sales. Amid revelations that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a data-industry executive who was suspected of being a Chinese intelligence source, Sen. Chris Coons wrote on X: “The more I learn about the insane relationship between the Trump Administration, Chinese spies, and AI billionaires, the more I’m convinced there is nothing this administration does that isn’t corrupt. Congress will investigate and get answers.” Loosening tech controls in this environment will be a tough sell.

   As for Trump, he has spent his second term swinging between threats and enticements with Beijing—ratcheting up tariffs one month, talking about a big deal the next. “That approach has yielded very little and is unlikely to yield a breakthrough over the next year,” Turpin said. “But it’s the style that President Trump prefers and I’m not aware of too many 80-year-olds that change their style even when it isn’t working.”

   The real danger at Shenzhen may be that Xi arrives thinking he has the upper hand over a weakened Trump, when what’s actually sitting across the table is a president who suspects his Chinese counterpart might just have cost him Congress.

   How do you think Beijing will read the midterm results, as an opportunity or a warning sign? Write to me at lingling.wei@wsj.com . Include your full name and location, and I might publish your response in an upcoming issue (if you’re reading this in your inbox, you can just hit reply).

Beijing Sees a Weakened Trump. It Risks Getting a Tougher Negotiator.
 
Plus, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang apologizes to employees and family, and Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong gets more prison time on foreign-collusion charges
 
 
President Trump campaigned in Mississippi for Republicans ahead of his party’s midterm losses. CHIP SOMODEVILLA/GETTY IMAGES
 

In November 2014, days after Democrats suffered a bruising midterm defeat, President Obama traveled to Beijing for an annual gathering of Pacific Rim leaders and a state visit. Xi Jinping, sensing his counterpart’s weakened position, subjected Obama to hours of lectures on Chinese history and governance.

 

President Trump is heading to Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit next week, following a midterm loss that was more sweeping than Obama’s. Democrats captured both the House and Senate in what amounted to a repudiation of his presidency. Xi will use the opportunity of hosting APEC to show off China’s tech-driven modernity, even as his team and Trump’s wrangle behind the scenes over plans for an unprecedented three-way meeting involving Trump, Xi and Russian leader Vladimir Putin.

Back then, “Xi felt confident that the United States under Obama’s leadership wasn’t going to confront the People’s Republic of China,” said Matt Turpin, a visiting fellow at the Hoover Institution who served on Trump’s National Security Council during his first term. China’s economy was still expanding at more than 7% at the time while the post-financial-crisis West struggled, and Washington still embraced free trade with China. The Chinese leader was riding high.

 

Trump—and China—in 2026 are different. China’s economy is in far worse shape than it was 12 years ago, and Xi faces his own sensitive political year in 2027, when a leadership reshuffle at the 21st Party Congress will demand his full attention. A volatile relationship with Washington would be the last thing he wants.

Since a trade agreement struck a year ago in the South Korean city of Busan, Beijing has fallen short of fulfilling its commitments on agricultural purchases and rare earth exports. In addition, China restricted diesel exports just weeks before the midterm elections. Even though Beijing said the move was aimed at ensuring domestic supply, analysts noted it compounded global energy pressures at a vulnerable political moment for Trump.

If that’s how Trump sees it, he has little motivation to offer Xi concessions, including on Taiwan, where Beijing earlier this year secured a freeze on U.S. arms sales and has been pressing for rhetorical policy shifts that favor its sovereignty claims over the island.

 

Trump’s choice of Stephen Miller, a hard-line immigration architect, to replace Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff also suggests he is more inclined to double down than moderate his approach after the defeat.

 

No ‘America Doves’

 

One alarming dynamic in the bilateral relationship is the absence of moderating voices on the Chinese side. There are only “America hawks” in the Chinese system, Turpin noted—“no ‘America doves.’” That’s even more pronounced under Xi’s consolidation of power, where the internal incentive is always to be tougher on the U.S., never softer.

 

That hawkish consensus is paired with a dangerous blind spot. “Chinese Communist Party leaders really don’t understand the relationship between the president and Congress,” Turpin said. “They largely mirror image and assume the U.S. political system works like theirs.”

On the U.S. side, Turpin expects Democratic congressional leadership to focus on investigating the last two years, uncovering corruption, going after the tech industry, and setting the stage for the 2028 presidential election. Unlike the final years of the Biden administration, when a Republican House worked with a Democratic White House to build a bipartisan consensus on China, Turpin said, the foreign policy energy is more likely to flow toward Israel, Iran and Russia.

 

But on one front, the new Democratic majority could make things harder for Beijing. 

 

China has long sought the elimination of U.S. restrictions on high-tech sales. Amid revelations that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a data-industry executive who was suspected of being a Chinese intelligence source, Sen. Chris Coons wrote on X: “The more I learn about the insane relationship between the Trump Administration, Chinese spies, and AI billionaires, the more I’m convinced there is nothing this administration does that isn’t corrupt. Congress will investigate and get answers.” Loosening tech controls in this environment will be a tough sell.

 

As for Trump, he has spent his second term swinging between threats and enticements with Beijing—ratcheting up tariffs one month, talking about a big deal the next. “That approach has yielded very little and is unlikely to yield a breakthrough over the next year,” Turpin said. “But it’s the style that President Trump prefers and I’m not aware of too many 80-year-olds that change their style even when it isn’t working.”

China in a Few Headlines

 

• Beijing blocked SoftBank’s $5.4 billion purchase of ABB’s robotics unit, citing data security and competition concerns, derailing Masayoshi Son’s physical AI ambitions.

 

• China’s October producer prices jumped 5.7%, the fastest rise in over four years, as energy costs surged, while consumer inflation cooled to 0.7%, below forecasts.

 

• Weak demand in the U.S. and China drove Volvo Cars’ global sales down 16% year-over-year to 141,656 through October, while electrified-vehicle sales fell 3%.

 
 
 

The Number

 
10 years
 

Imprisoned Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong received an additional National Security Law sentence after pleading guilty to foreign collusion charges—a move human rights groups condemned as politically motivated to keep him detained.

 
 
 

A Closer Look

 
 
Source: Center for Strategic and International Studies (Agreements); Flanders Marine Institute (Maritime boundaries) ASHLEY CAI/WSJ
 

Australia’s proactive diplomacy and new security pacts with Western-friendly Pacific nations (Vanuatu, Fiji, and Papua New Guinea) have blunted China’s regional momentum, reinforcing broader U.S. efforts to counter Beijing in the Pacific.

 
 
 

Reader Responses

 

Last week, we asked how long Beijing can have both—wanting foreign capital but unwilling to give foreign investors equal access to information. Readers shared their thoughts:

 

“As an international investor, the problems you highlight in your article show the dangers of information asymmetry for investors. In the long run, this can only mean that international investors (like myself) will be hurt by selectively published information. Chinese companies, however, are most likely unable to become more transparent because they can’t upset local politicians. So while Alibaba, Tencent and other companies seem like interesting investments, I would probably have to give them a hard pass now to avoid getting caught in potential bad news in the future.”—Chris Niksch, Germany

 

“Beijing has repeatedly shown that they will not shy away from cutting information flow that makes the data (or country) look bad. China’s pattern of prioritizing narrative control over transparency makes clear which it values more. For foreign investors, that just seems to create this never-ending cycle of the less transparent the market becomes, the larger the risk premium investors demand, which in turn makes attracting durable foreign capital harder.”—Charles Dodd, Texas

 

“I think the ability to segment information between Chinese and foreign investors has already run its course. The recent drop in value of Chinese stocks is evidence of skepticism that the numbers reported by Chinese companies (and the government) are accurate and reliable. Once trust is gone, how can you justify giving them money?”—Steve Andrews, California

 

(Responses have been condensed and edited.)

 
 
 

A Name in the News

 
 
Jensen Huang with his family in 2007: from left, daughter Madison, wife Lori and son Spencer. THU HOANG LY/MERCURY NEWS/GETTY IMAGES
 

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang apologized to employees for marital infidelity in a note that also addressed his family. The episode comes amid reports that the U.S. government suspects a former executive he was involved with of sharing information with Chinese intelligence, prompting Nvidia’s board to open an investigation into whether Huang was targeted.
